analysis.evidence: יַהְוֶה is the subject of וַיֹּאמֶר. The first-person phrase רוּחִי (“my spirit”) in the following clause marks it as his direct speech.
analysis.morphology: Qal wayyiqtol, third person masculine singular, with prefixed וַ־

analysis.evidence: In וַיֹּאמֶר יַהְוֶה (“and Yahweh said”), יַהְוֶה names the speaker, who refers to his own spirit as רוּחִי (“my spirit”).
analysis.morphology: Singular proper noun without a prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: Personal name of the God of Israel

analysis.evidence: לֹא precedes יָדוֹן, whose subject is רוּחִי (“my spirit”). With לְעֹלָם (“forever”), the clause declares that the action will not continue forever.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew negative particle with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: וַיֹּאמֶר יַהְוֶה identifies Yahweh as the speaker, so the suffix ־ִי in רוּחִי identifies the spirit as his. The clause contrasts his spirit with the human described as בָשָׂר, “flesh.”
analysis.morphology: Common-gender singular noun in the construct state with the first-person singular possessive suffix ־ִי.

analysis.evidence: בָאָדָם refers to humanity collectively. The singular הוּא in הוּא בָשָׂר (“he is flesh”) refers back to אָדָם, and the statement about the days of human life applies to humanity as a whole.
analysis.morphology: Preposition בְּ with the definite article, followed by a masculine singular absolute noun used collectively.

analysis.evidence: In לֹא יָדוֹן רוּחִי בָאָדָם לְעֹלָם, the negation rules out the action continuing forever. The closing clause gives a definite span of 120 years.
analysis.morphology: Preposition לְ prefixed to a masculine singular absolute noun, used adverbially.
analysis.sense: duration with no stated endpoint (in context)

analysis.evidence: In בְּשַׁגַּם הוּא בָשָׂר, “because he too is flesh,” הוּא refers back to הָאָדָם and supplies “he.” גַּם supplies “too.” The clause gives the reason for the preceding limit on God's spirit in humankind.
analysis.morphology: The prefixed preposition בְּ־ and relative particle שַׁ־ introduce a causal clause. גַּם is an indeclinable additive adverb meaning “too.”

analysis.evidence: In הוּא בָשָׂר, “he is flesh,” הוּא refers back to הָאָדָם, “humankind.” The pronoun supplies the subject, and בָשָׂר is its predicate.
analysis.morphology: Independent third-person masculine singular personal pronoun, without prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: In הוּא בָשָׂר, “he is flesh,” הוּא refers to humankind (הָאָדָם). The contrast with רוּחִי, “my spirit,” and the limit of 120 years on “his days” give flesh its sense of human mortality.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular absolute noun, used as a predicate, with no prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: flesh: man as weak and mortal

analysis.evidence: וְהָיוּ agrees with the plural subject יָמָיו, “his days,” and links it to the stated duration מֵאָה וְעֶשְׂרִים שָׁנָה, “one hundred and twenty years.”
analysis.morphology: Qal perfect, third person common plural, with prefixed conjunction וְ (weqatal), expressing future time.
analysis.sense: to be in a state or condition

analysis.evidence: The suffix in יָמָיו refers back to הָאָדָם, humankind, expressed as a masculine singular. The clause וְהָיוּ יָמָיו מֵאָה וְעֶשְׂרִים שָׁנָה measures those days as 120 years, so the plural denotes the span allotted to humankind.
analysis.morphology: Masculine plural noun in the construct state with a third-person masculine singular possessive suffix.
analysis.sense: (pl.) days of a life, a reign or an age

analysis.evidence: In מֵאָה וְעֶשְׂרִים שָׁנָה, מֵאָה supplies the hundred and וְעֶשְׂרִים adds twenty, giving a total of 120 years.
analysis.morphology: Cardinal numeral, singular absolute, without prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: In מֵאָה וְעֶשְׂרִים שָׁנָה, the conjunction joins twenty to one hundred, giving a total of 120 years.
analysis.morphology: Conjunction וְ prefixed to a cardinal numeral, common gender, plural absolute.

analysis.evidence: וְהָיוּ יָמָיו means “his days shall be.” The phrase מֵאָה וְעֶשְׂרִים שָׁנָה gives the measure of those days as 120 years. The Hebrew noun is singular after the compound numeral.
analysis.morphology: Feminine singular absolute noun, without prefix or suffix.
